text: Τὰ μετάφρενα. Sunt quæ alii vocant μεταχένια. Suid. ὁ μεταξὺ τῶν ὤμων τόπος: Locus inter humeros: terga, dorsum. Suppletque Portus, quod a tergo præcordiis est objectum: sumpsitque ex Vaticano, cujus hæc sunt verba, Μετάφρενα. τὰ νῶτα, ὅτι ἐξόπισθεν τῶν φρενῶν κεῖται· φρένες δὲ, ὑμένες εἰσὶ μεταξὺ τῆς καρδίας καὶ τοῦ ἥπατος· Quod retro τῶν φρενῶν posita sunt: φρένες enim membranæ sunt inter cor. et jecur. Τὸ, ἐν χλωρότητι χρυσίου, quod Syxt. interpres reddere maluit, Hilarium secutus et August., in viriditate auri, quam quod Vulg. reddiderat, non probo. Liquet enim virorem et viriditatem non apte dici de auro (quidquid Hilarius, vigorem quemdam æternum putet ea voce significari), sed potius fulvorem et pallorem, qui auri color optimus est: auctor enim Galenus χλωρὸν ἀντὶ ὠχροῦ sumi; nec Hyppocrates aliter usurpat. Plinius quoque sic accepit apud Dioscorid. lib. iii, cap. 79, De Smyrnio, φλοιὸν ἔχουσα ἔξωθεν μὲν μέλανα, ἔνδοθεν δὲ χλωρὸν ἢ ὑπόλευκον· ipse sic vertit lib. xxvii, cap. 13: Cortex ejus foris niger, intus pallidus. Cum viride saturum significare volunt auctores, πρασοειδὲς vocare solent, et ὡσεὶ πράσον, quasi porro simile, convenitque quibusdam lapillis et herbis; auro, nunquam.
anchorLine: ρί· τὰ δὲ νοούμενα, φημὶ δὴ τὰ μετάφρενα (a),
en: Metaphrena: some call these metaxenia (sic). Suidas: the place between the shoulders, i.e. the region between the shoulders: the back, the dorsum. Portus adds: what lies behind the midriff; and he took it from the Vatican codex, whose words are: 'Metaphrena: the back, because it lies behind the phrenes; the phrenes are membranes between the heart and the liver.' That is, the parts situated behind the phrenes: for the phrenes are membranes between heart and liver. As for 'in the greenness (chlorotes) of gold,' which the Sixtine translator preferred to render, following Hilary and Augustine, 'in the viridity of gold,' rather than the Vulgate's rendering, the editor does not approve. For it is clear that verdure and greenness are not aptly said of gold (whatever Hilary may think, that some eternal vigor is signified by that word), but rather its yellow and pallor, which is the best colour of gold: for Galen is the authority that chloron is taken for ochron (pale); nor does Hippocrates use it otherwise. Pliny too understood it so in Dioscorides, book iii, ch. 79, on Smyrnium: 'having a bark black outside, chloron or whitish within'; he himself renders it, book xxvii, ch. 13: 'Its bark is black outside, pale inside.' When writers mean to signify a deep green they usually say leek-green (prasoeides), and 'as if leek-like'; it suits certain stones and herbs, never gold.

text: Καὶ ὡς ῥοθίζας κινήσεις. Quin sit mendum in illa voce, nullus dubito. Sit forte ῥοθίας, vel ῥοθιαζούσας, quod etiam verbum agnoscit Hesych. quasi tremente fluctus commotiones procellamque; ut alia aliam vocem Maximus explicet. Hoc enim præstant maris elationes, ut fluctus sic impetu assurgentibus, tumque eadem vi subsidentibus, aliisque alios intercipientibus ac se mutuo collidentibus, allisisque ad littora ipsasque rupes ac cautes, strepitus ejusmodi ac fragor procul reboet, qui terrorem ac stuporem injiciat: quæ omnia quasi alio in mari procul considerat, qui ipse in tranquillo contemplationis mari, velut ad clavum quiete sedens illique indormiens, vehitur.
anchorLine: πῶν μετεωρισμοὺς, καὶ ὡς ῥοθίζας κινήσεις (b), τὰ
en: 'And as [he considers] ῥοθίζας motions.' I have no doubt that there is an error in that word. Perhaps it should be ῥοθίας, or ῥοθιαζούσας, a verb Hesychius also recognizes: as if 'trembling commotions of the waves' and storm; so that Maximus would explain one word by another. For the swellings of the sea produce this: the waves rise with such force, then sink with the same force, others cutting off others and dashing against one another and thrown against the shores and the very rocks and reefs, so that such a noise and crash resounds from afar, which strikes terror and stupor. All this he observes as though in another sea, far off, he who himself is carried on the tranquil sea of contemplation, sitting quietly at the helm, as it were, and sleeping there.

text: Μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ἡγεμονικοῦ. Quem Maximus spiritum ἡγεμονικὸν hic vocat, ipse est quem Paulus Ephes. iv, 21, spiritum τοῦ νοὸς (mentis) vocat, et hortatur eo renovari; quod mens ipsa τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν in homine sit: quod scilicet in eo principale est ac imperio pollet: quæ, cum ipsa ex se fixa sit veri contemplatione, orationem ea fultam constantem, uniusque rationis (μονολόγιστον) reddat: τὸ προαιρετικὸν vero (velut dicas, arbitrarium) voluntatem, quæ pro hoc statu instabilis sit, exque alia in aliam mutatur pro rerum objectarum ac cogitationum varietate, inque eas affectione.
anchorLine: ματος ἡγεμονικοῦ (c) · ἄνευ δὲ θεωρίας, ὡς σάρξ
en: 'With the governing spirit.' The spirit that Maximus here calls 'hegemonic' is the very one Paul, in Ephesians iv, 21, calls the spirit of the mind, and he urges that we be renewed by it; for the mind itself is the hegemonic part in man, that is, it is the principal part in him and holds sway. When it is itself fixed on the contemplation of the truth, it makes prayer supported by it steady and of a single reasoning (monologiston). But the 'elective' faculty (as one might say, the arbitrary), that is the will, which in this state is unstable and shifts from one thing to another according to the variety of the objects and thoughts presented, and to the affection toward them.

text: Σαρκὶ παραμένειν. Græca vulgata, ἐπιμένειν ἐν τῇ σαρκί. Habent tamen codex Alexandrinus et Chrysost. in Expositione, ἐπιμένειν σαρκὶ, absque propositione, quæ nec admodum necessaria est, cum ejus vim habeat verbum compositum, sitque idem ἐπιμένειν atque ἐμμένειν· τὸ, παραμένειν Maximi magis respuit, habetque emphasin: permanere in carne, nec ab ea disjungi.
anchorLine: εὐδοκεῖ μᾶλλον σαρκὶ παραμένειν (d) · καὶ διὰ τὴν
en: 'To remain with the flesh.' The common Greek text reads 'to abide in the flesh.' Yet the Alexandrian codex and Chrysostom in his Exposition have 'to abide (with) the flesh' without the preposition, which is hardly necessary, since the compound verb carries its force, and 'epimenein' is the same as 'emmenein.' The 'paramenein' of Maximus rather rejects the preposition and has emphasis: to remain in the flesh and not be separated from it.

text: Νεοτελὴς νοῦς. Quasi recens ad perfectionem initiatus, eamque novum adeptus; etsi necdum in illa satis probatus. Suid. νεοτελής, νεωστὶ τετελειωμένος· quod Thesaurus Hesychio ascribit, cum sit solum Suidæ, redditque. Recens absolutus: non satis bene Portus, Recens confectus. Vox enim illa, qua una Suid. alteram explicavit, quamdam absolutionem sonat et consummationem, non solam effectionem; de qua multa Budæus in Comment.
anchorLine: τὰ ἐκείνης ἐσθίειν ἀνέχεται· οὔτε νεοτελὴς νοῦς (e)
en: 'Newly perfected mind.' As one recently initiated to perfection and having newly obtained it, though not yet sufficiently proved in it. Suidas: 'neoteles: newly completed'; which the Thesaurus ascribes to Hesychius, although it is only Suidas's, and renders it 'recently finished/absolved.' Portus's 'recently completed (confectus)' is not quite right. For that word, by which Suidas alone explained the other, signifies a kind of absolution and consummation, not merely making; on which Budaeus has much in his Commentary.
